record.paper_title: On Open Problems in Biological Network Visualization
record.context_brief: integrated layouts for overlapping network types
record.original_question: Given two biological networks that describe different functional aspects of the same cell, tissue, or organism, model each as a cluster graph C1=(G1,T1) and C2=(G2,T2) of cluster depth 2, with a mapping function Phi from clusters or entities in one network to clusters or entities in the other. The mapping may be 1:1, 1:n, or n:m, and the union layout should contain G1, G2, and the edges induced by the mapping. How can one generate a joint layout that reveals interactions between the networks, displays the mapping, respects the clusters and the conventional layout of each network, integrates disconnected components of one network into the layout of the other when appropriate, and balances preservation of a given layout or mental map for G1 against obtaining a better representation of G2?

evidence.quote: We need a representation of combined networks in which the conventional layouts (there may be several different ones) of each of these networks need to be respected.
Moreover, some groups of nodes in one network may belong to groups of nodes in another network. This mapping (which may be a 1:1, 1 : n, or n : m mapping) needs to be displayed in the layout.
Generate a layout π(G) of the union graph G = G1 ∪ G2 ∪ G[F], where F denotes the edges induced by the mapping, respecting the clusters as well as the conventional layouts of each of these networks.

artifact.category_tag: Graph drawing and biological network visualization
artifact.status_search_result: The problem of producing integrated, cluster-respecting joint layouts of two biological networks linked by a 1:1/1:n/n:m mapping, while preserving each network's conventional layout and balancing mental-map preservation against improved drawing quality, does not appear to be resolved. Existing tools (Cytoscape plug-ins, multilevel gamma-clustering layouts, multilevel layouts for physical/genetic interactions, Metabopolis, CAbiNet) address related sub-problems such as clustered layouts or joint embeddings, but recent surveys still list integrated multi-network layout with mapping-edge constraints among open challenges in biological network visualization.

status_evidence.title: An introduction to and survey of biological network visualization
status_evidence.snippet: Open challenges include the lack of visualization tools that integrate more advanced network analysis techniques and combined representations of multiple networks.
status_evidence.claim: Recent survey indicates integrated multi-network visualization remains an open challenge.

status_evidence.title: A Multilevel Gamma-Clustering Layout Algorithm for Visualization of Biological Networks
status_evidence.snippet: MLGA identifies cluster structure, transforms the network to a tree, and applies a force-directed algorithm.
status_evidence.claim: Existing clustered-layout methods treat single networks, not paired networks with inter-network mappings.

status_evidence.title: CAbiNet: joint clustering and visualization of cells and genes
status_evidence.snippet: Produces a joint visualization and co-clustering of cells and genes in a planar embedding.
status_evidence.claim: Joint visualizations exist for specific bipartite biological data but do not address the general integrated cluster-graph layout problem with conventional-layout preservation.
